lines.text: # Faculty of Computing — Initial Site & Feasibility Survey
Stage: university-survey (early feasibility, concurrent with five peer faculties)
Site: flat, level ground, approx. 60 m x 60 m (3,600 m² gross plot)
Soil: stratified (layered), generally suitable for standard shallow spread-footing foundations
## 1. Terrain and site conditions — approach
**Ground and foundations.** The plot is flat and level, so no significant cut-and-fill
balancing or retaining is anticipated. The soil is stratified, which is the one condition
that actually needs attention: layered soils can carry a *weaker* stratum beneath a
stiffer one, and a spread footing bearing on the upper layer can punch through or settle
differentially if the layer boundary is shallow and sloping.
Approach:
- Confirm the layer sequence and depth of each stratum with a small borehole/cable-percussion
investigation (say 3–4 boreholes to ~8–10 m, plus a couple of dynamic probe tests) before
fixing foundation levels. This is cheap insurance and is the single most valuable
pre-design action on this site.
- Assume standard shallow reinforced-concrete pad/strip footings bearing on the competent
upper stratum, founded at a uniform depth below the layer boundary where possible, so all
footings of a given structure bear on the *same* material. Where the boundary is
irregular, step the footings or locally deepen to a consistent bearing stratum rather
than letting part of the building sit on a different layer.
- Design for a modest differential-settlement allowance and use a reinforced ground beam /
tie-beam grid to stitch pad footings together, which is standard practice and also
stiffens the building against the layered-soil risk.
- No evidence of a high water table is given; still, keep footings above the seasonal
water table and provide standard damp-proofing (DPM under slab, DPC at wall base) since
a cafeteria and ground-floor teaching spaces are moisture-sensitive.
- Flat ground means surface drainage must be designed, not assumed: the plot is level, so
rainwater will pond. Provide a positive fall on external paving away from the building
and a perimeter surface-water drainage line (channel drains / gullies) connected to the
site system, plus a fall on the roof to outlets.
**Orientation and climate.** With a square, unconstrained plot, orientation is a free
choice and should be used deliberately: long teaching elevations oriented to minimise
low-angle east/west solar gain, with the cafeteria and its glazing placed to take
daylight without direct afternoon sun on the dining area. Deep roof overhangs or external
shading on the sun-facing elevations reduce cooling load — relevant because computing
teaching spaces have high internal heat gains from equipment and occupancy.
**Access and servicing.** Assume a perimeter road/emergency vehicle access loop is
possible within the plot, with the main entrance and pedestrian approach on one edge and
a service/kitchen yard on the opposite edge so that deliveries, waste and kitchen extract
do not cross the main student circulation.
## 2. Zoning and footprint concept
Concept: a compact, two-storey (part three-storey) teaching block with a clearly separated
cafeteria wing, arranged around a small courtyard/arrival space. Rough split of the
3,600 m² plot:
| Zone | Approx. share | Content |
| Main teaching block | ~40% footprint | Lecture halls, classrooms, seminar rooms, stacked vertically |
| Staff/administration | within main block | Offices, meeting rooms, staff facilities |
| Cafeteria/canteen wing | ~15% footprint | Dining hall + kitchen + servery + stores + waste |
| Circulation / atrium / stairs | within blocks | Vertical and horizontal circulation, toilets |
| External | remainder | Arrival plaza, courtyard, service yard, planting, drainage |
Zoning logic:
- **Teaching block** placed toward the quieter, main-approach side; large-span lecture
halls at ground and first floor where column-free volume is easiest to achieve, smaller
classrooms and offices above/beside.
- **Cafeteria wing** placed on a separate edge with its own service yard, delivery access
and a dedicated kitchen extract route to roof. It is deliberately *structurally and
fire-separated* from the teaching block (see §4) — a cafeteria is the highest-hazard,
highest-servicing element of the brief and should not be buried in the middle of the plan.
- **Kitchen** at the back of the cafeteria wing against the service yard, dining hall at
the front with daylight; servery between them. This keeps the grease-producing zone away
from teaching spaces and gives a short, direct extract duct run to a roof discharge.
- **Vertical stacking** of teaching spaces keeps the footprint compact, preserves external
space on a modest 60 m × 60 m plot, and shortens service runs. A single-storey scheme
would consume most of the plot and leave no room for the service yard and drainage.
- **Structural grid** set out on a regular bay (e.g. ~7.5–8.5 m) so that classrooms,
offices and the cafeteria dining hall all land on the same grid, with lecture halls
spanning two bays where a clear span is needed.
## 3. Primary construction materials — building generally
- **Structure:** reinforced-concrete frame (columns, beams, flat or beam-and-block slabs)
on shallow pad/strip footings. Rationale: the site suits shallow foundations, concrete
is robust and low-maintenance, gives good fire resistance and acoustic mass between
stacked teaching floors, and handles the layered-soil differential-settlement risk well
when tied together with ground beams. Long-span lecture halls can use either deeper
concrete beams or a steel roof structure over the concrete frame.
- **Upper floors / roofs:** concrete slabs for teaching floors (acoustic separation,
vibration control for equipment); lightweight steel or timber roof structure over the
top floor with a warm flat roof (insulated, membrane-covered) — flat roofs suit the
square plot and give clean roof space for the kitchen extract discharge and any plant.
- **External walls:** insulated masonry cavity wall (blockwork inner leaf, brick or
rendered block outer leaf) as the baseline — durable, low-maintenance, good acoustic and
thermal mass, familiar local construction. Rainscreen or lightweight cladding panels
acceptable on feature elevations and around the cafeteria glazing.
- **Glazing:** aluminium-framed double-glazed units with solar-control glass on
sun-facing elevations; openable sections for natural ventilation in classrooms, with
mechanical ventilation/comfort cooling where equipment loads demand it.
- **Internal partitions:** blockwork or stud-and-board partitions with acoustic insulation
between teaching rooms; fire-rated boards where compartment lines require it.
- **Finishes:** hard-wearing, low-maintenance — sealed concrete or vinyl/ceramic floors in
circulation and teaching, painted plasterboard/blockwork walls, suspended ceilings in
offices and corridors to conceal services.
## 4. Cafeteria/canteen — specific materials and construction
The cafeteria is the element of the brief with the most demanding combination of
requirements: **structural span** (column-free dining), **fire rating** (cooking hazard),
**hygiene and moisture resistance** (food preparation, washing, steam, grease), and
**maintenance** (heavy use, cleaning chemicals, grease).
**Structural span.** Dining halls read best column-free. Use a long-span floor/roof over
the dining area — either a deep reinforced-concrete beam/ribbed slab or, more economically
for a clear span, a steel roof structure (portal or truss) with a metal deck and
insulated membrane roof. Kitchen and servery can be on the normal column grid; only the
dining hall needs the clear span.
**Fire rating.** The kitchen is a fire compartment in its own right:
- Fire-rated wall (typically 60–120 min, per local code) separating kitchen from dining
hall and from any adjacent teaching/staff space, with self-closing fire doors.
- Fire-rated ceiling/roof construction over the kitchen and over the extract route.
- **Kitchen grease-laden exhaust** is the specific hazard: grease vapour deposits on duct
walls and can ignite from a cookline flare-up, and fire can travel *inside* the duct
through otherwise fire-separated compartments. Therefore:
- a dedicated, continuously welded or flanged liquid-tight **grease duct** (not ordinary
galvanised spiral duct), with access doors at every change of direction for cleaning;
- the duct enclosed in a fire-rated shaft or wrapped with a listed fire-rated system
where it passes through or adjacent to other occupancies, terminating well clear of
air intakes, windows and combustible roof build-up;
- a dedicated kitchen suppression system (hood + duct) interlocked to shut down the
supply fan and fuel supply, plus a grease trap/interceptor on the kitchen drainage.
- This drives ceiling void depth, roof penetrations and shaft locations, so it is fixed
early in the zoning layout (see §2) rather than retrofitted.
**Hygiene and moisture resistance.** Kitchen and servery need impervious, washable,
non-absorbent surfaces:
- Floors: slip-resistant ceramic/quarry tile or epoxy-resin screed with coved skirting to
walls, laid to falls to trapped floor drains.
- Walls: ceramic tiling or smooth, washable, impact-resistant panel/board to splash and
working heights; sealed, easily cleaned junctions.
- Ceilings: moisture-resistant, wipe-clean panels or sealed painted substrate; avoid
exposed absorbent surfaces and ledges that trap grease.
- Stainless-steel worktops, sinks and equipment stands; stainless or coated-metal
ductwork and hoods.
- Dining hall: hard-wearing, easily mopped floor (vinyl, tile or sealed concrete), durable
wipe-clean wall finishes, and moisture-tolerant ceiling — less stringent than the
kitchen but still specified for spillage and cleaning.
**Maintenance.** All cafeteria finishes chosen for cleanability and repairability:
replaceable floor tiles, accessible duct cleaning doors, removable ceiling panels for
service access, and durable, scrubbable wall finishes. Kitchen extract and grease
interceptor require a scheduled cleaning regime — this is a maintenance commitment, not
just a design item, and should be recorded in the facilities brief.
**Services.** Kitchen needs high-capacity mechanical extract, generous cold water and hot
water supply, gas or electric cooking supply, and a drainage line sized for grease-laden
waste with an interceptor. Dining hall needs good ventilation and daylight. All of this
concentrates services in one wing, which is another reason to zone the cafeteria as a
distinct, service-rich block.
## 5. Risks and open items for the next stage
- Confirm stratified-soil layer depths and bearing capacity by ground investigation before
fixing foundation design; the layered profile is the main geotechnical uncertainty.
- Confirm local fire code compartment sizes and required fire resistance periods for the
kitchen and its extract duct.
- Confirm kitchen fuel type (gas vs electric) — affects services, ventilation and
suppression design.
- Confirm whether the plot's flat, level ground has any existing drainage outfall; if not,
a site attenuation/soakaway strategy may be needed.
- Confirm planning/height limits, which will cap the vertical stacking strategy.
## 6. Influence of peer findings (open_questions)
At the time this survey was written, one live finding was present in `open_questions`:
`finding-computing-1647d8c9` — the cafeteria kitchen grease-laden exhaust hazard
(grease duct specification, fire-rated enclosure, kitchen suppression, grease interceptor,
fire separation of kitchen from dining and teaching spaces).
That finding is **my own**, raised by me earlier in this task, so it is not a peer's
finding. It did, however, directly shape this survey: §2 places the kitchen against the
service yard with a short, direct extract route to roof and separates the cafeteria wing
from the teaching block, and §4 specifies the welded/flanged grease duct, fire-rated
shaft/wrap, hood-and-duct suppression interlocked to fan and fuel, grease interceptor, and
fire-rated kitchen separation. No *peer* finding had arrived by the time this survey was
written, so no peer finding influenced anything here; if a peer finding arrives later, the
kitchen extract and fire-separation provisions above are the parts of this survey most
likely to need review.
